bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price inflation - cotton price volatility — Cotton is the primary raw material and volatility in cotton prices may adversely affect profitability. The year showed this directly: a sharp reduction in global cotton prices in the first half left prices at multi-year lows in domestic and international markets. The Company monitors cotton price trends and maintains a disciplined inventory approach.
- Climate change and raw material availability — Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Cotton dependence makes operations vulnerable to erratic rainfall, droughts, floods and rising temperatures, which can hit cotton production, fibre quality, availability and prices, causing supply-chain disruption and higher procurement costs. Mitigation is supplier diversification, procurement planning, strategic inventory and sustainable agricultural practices.
- Tariff and trade policy risk — Uncertainties in global trade policies and tariff structures may weaken export demand and pressure margins. In FY 2025-26 U.S. tariff uncertainty subdued demand in the first half and cut fabric sales by 7.35%; management is diversifying into lower-tariff markets, strengthening presence in EU and UK regions and rebalancing toward domestic demand.
- Export and foreign-currency concentration — Exports were 61.87% of total revenue (Rs. 1988.43 Crores, down 5.81% on the year), so rupee fluctuations directly affect earnings and any export-market shock transmits straight to the top line. The Company follows a structured forex hedging policy.
- Customer concentration — Dependence on a limited number of customers may lead to revenue fluctuations; the Company's stated response is to keep diversifying its customer base across geographies to reduce reliance on any single customer.
- Competition risk — Increased competition may reduce returns on investment, market share and profit margins. Mitigated through value addition, product quality, customer service, a diverse product portfolio, cost efficiency and a widening customer base.
- Energy intensity and the transition to renewable energy — Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Textile manufacturing is highly energy intensive across spinning, knitting, weaving and processing; rising energy costs, dependence on conventional fuels and increasing regulatory focus on carbon emissions may hit operational efficiency and profitability if consumption is not managed. Mitigation is process optimisation, energy-efficient machinery, preventive maintenance, waste heat recovery and a rising renewable share.
- Water stewardship and effluent management — Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Water is critical to dyeing and finishing; growing water scarcity, stricter environmental regulation and stakeholder expectations may affect operational continuity and compliance. Mitigation is process optimisation, recycling and reuse of treated wastewater, effluent treatment, rainwater harvesting and consumption monitoring.

business.body: Demand improved in Q4 across both domestic and export — driven by US tariff removal, restocking across downstream channels, and longer transit times prompting earlier buying. outlook.body: The Company is undertaking a strategic capacity expansion to strengthen its integrated textile operations and enhance its presence in value-added segments. The expansion adds 22,400 MTPA of spinning capacity and weaving and finishing fabric capacity of 35 million metres per annum, with the MD&A chart showing spinning going from 110.0 to 132.4 thousand tonnes per annum (+20%) and weaving and finishing fabric from 40.0 to 75.0 million metres per annum (+88%) by FY 2026-27. Nearly 60% of the incremental spinning output is expected to be used in-house for fabric manufacturing, which management says should improve the margin profile while broadening the product portfolio, opening new markets and shifting mix toward premium and value-added offerings. outlook.body:
- Management expects improving demand conditions, better price realisations and a gradual improvement in industry spreads to provide a favourable backdrop for the next phase of growth.
- Conditions improved in the fourth quarter as trade restrictions eased, downstream channel inventories were replenished and yarn prices recovered, producing the highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs. 859.8 Crores on strong capacity utilisation and improved realisations.
- The first half was hit by subdued demand following U.S. tariff-related developments and multi-year-low cotton prices in domestic and international markets; the second half brought geopolitical turmoil in West Asia that created supply-chain bottlenecks, raised freight costs, extended transit timelines and pressured input costs.
- Proposed free trade agreements, particularly with the UK and the European Union, are expected to unlock new opportunities for Indian textile exporters by improving market access and addressing duty disadvantages versus competitors.
- Global sourcing preferences are shifting toward India as labour costs rise in Vietnam and political unrest continues in Bangladesh, while potential US tariffs on Chinese textiles may divert further orders to Indian producers.
- Government initiatives, including the PLI Scheme, Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel (MITRA) Parks and the promotion of Kasturi Cotton as a cleaner and traceable alternative, are expected to support competitiveness and investment.
- India remained the world's second-largest producer and third-largest exporter of textiles and apparel, with a domestic market growing 11.38%, exports of approximately USD 37 billion and a stated USD 100 billion export target by FY 2029-30.
- The Indian textile and apparel market is projected to reach USD 656.31 billion by FY 2033-34 and the global market USD 4,016.50 billion by FY 2033-34 at a 7.35% CAGR, with growth becoming increasingly value-driven and innovation-led and led by value-added segments such as technical textiles and man-made fibres.
- Industry-level headwinds flagged include supply-chain and logistics fragmentation, tariff and non-tariff barriers, technological gaps in domestic weaving and processing machinery, labour and skill shortages, and tighter environmental regulation.
- India's real GDP is projected to grow by 6.9% in FY 2026-27, and global growth by around 3.1% in CY 2026, with trade growth moderating on tariffs and geopolitics.
- Cotton yield productivity below global benchmarks remains a structural constraint, with government programmes such as the proposed Mission for Cotton Productivity aimed at improving it.

risks.risk: Raw material price inflation - cotton price volatility
risks.note: Cotton is the primary raw material and volatility in cotton prices may adversely affect profitability. The year showed this directly: a sharp reduction in global cotton prices in the first half left prices at multi-year lows in domestic and international markets. The Company monitors cotton price trends and maintains a disciplined inventory approach.

risks.risk: Climate change and raw material availability
risks.note: Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Cotton dependence makes operations vulnerable to erratic rainfall, droughts, floods and rising temperatures, which can hit cotton production, fibre quality, availability and prices, causing supply-chain disruption and higher procurement costs. Mitigation is supplier diversification, procurement planning, strategic inventory and sustainable agricultural practices.

Uncertainties in global trade policies and tariff structures may weaken export demand and pressure margins. In FY 2025-26 U.S. tariff uncertainty subdued demand in the first half and cut fabric sales by 7.35%; management is diversifying into lower-tariff markets, strengthening presence in EU and UK regions and rebalancing toward domestic demand.

Exports were 61.87% of total revenue (Rs. 1988.43 Crores, down 5.81% on the year), so rupee fluctuations directly affect earnings and any export-market shock transmits straight to the top line. The Company follows a structured forex hedging policy.

Dependence on a limited number of customers may lead to revenue fluctuations; the Company's stated response is to keep diversifying its customer base across geographies to reduce reliance on any single customer.

Increased competition may reduce returns on investment, market share and profit margins. Mitigated through value addition, product quality, customer service, a diverse product portfolio, cost efficiency and a widening customer base.

risks.risk: Energy intensity and the transition to renewable energy
risks.note: Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Textile manufacturing is highly energy intensive across spinning, knitting, weaving and processing; rising energy costs, dependence on conventional fuels and increasing regulatory focus on carbon emissions may hit operational efficiency and profitability if consumption is not managed. Mitigation is process optimisation, energy-efficient machinery, preventive maintenance, waste heat recovery and a rising renewable share.

Flagged as a material BRSR risk with negative financial implications. Water is critical to dyeing and finishing; growing water scarcity, stricter environmental regulation and stakeholder expectations may affect operational continuity and compliance. Mitigation is process optimisation, recycling and reuse of treated wastewater, effluent treatment, rainwater harvesting and consumption monitoring.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company makes cotton and blended yarns, knitted fabrics and finished woven fabrics from two manufacturing units at Bhilwara and Chittorgarh, and reports a single business segment, Textiles. It sells to apparel, home-textile, industrial-textile, healthcare and protective-clothing users and to retail and export houses in both domestic and international markets, with exports contributing 61.87% of turnover. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management expects improving demand conditions, better price realisations and a gradual improvement in industry spreads to provide a favourable backdrop for the next phase of growth.
- Conditions improved in the fourth quarter as trade restrictions eased, downstream channel inventories were replenished and yarn prices recovered, producing the highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs. 859.8 Crores on strong capacity utilisation and improved realisations.
- The first half was hit by subdued demand following U.S. tariff-related developments and multi-year-low cotton prices in domestic and international markets; the second half brought geopolitical turmoil in West Asia that created supply-chain bottlenecks, raised freight costs, extended transit timelines and pressured input costs.
- Proposed free trade agreements, particularly with the UK and the European Union, are expected to unlock new opportunities for Indian textile exporters by improving market access and addressing duty disadvantages versus competitors.
- Global sourcing preferences are shifting toward India as labour costs rise in Vietnam and political unrest continues in Bangladesh, while potential US tariffs on Chinese textiles may divert further orders to Indian producers.
- Government initiatives, including the PLI Scheme, Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel (MITRA) Parks and the promotion of Kasturi Cotton as a cleaner and traceable alternative, are expected to support competitiveness and investment.
- India remained the world's second-largest producer and third-largest exporter of textiles and apparel, with a domestic market growing 11.38%, exports of approximately USD 37 billion and a stated USD 100 billion export target by FY 2029-30.
- The Indian textile and apparel market is projected to reach USD 656.31 billion by FY 2033-34 and the global market USD 4,016.50 billion by FY 2033-34 at a 7.35% CAGR, with growth becoming increasingly value-driven and innovation-led and led by value-added segments such as technical textiles and man-made fibres.
- Industry-level headwinds flagged include supply-chain and logistics fragmentation, tariff and non-tariff barriers, technological gaps in domestic weaving and processing machinery, labour and skill shortages, and tighter environmental regulation.
- India's real GDP is projected to grow by 6.9% in FY 2026-27, and global growth by around 3.1% in CY 2026, with trade growth moderating on tariffs and geopolitics.
- Cotton yield productivity below global benchmarks remains a structural constraint, with government programmes such as the proposed Mission for Cotton Productivity aimed at improving it.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Company is undertaking a strategic capacity expansion to strengthen its integrated textile operations and enhance its presence in value-added segments. The expansion adds 22,400 MTPA of spinning capacity and weaving and finishing fabric capacity of 35 million metres per annum, with the MD&A chart showing spinning going from 110.0 to 132.4 thousand tonnes per annum (+20%) and weaving and finishing fabric from 40.0 to 75.0 million metres per annum (+88%) by FY 2026-27. Nearly 60% of the incremental spinning output is expected to be used in-house for fabric manufacturing, which management says should improve the margin profile while broadening the product portfolio, opening new markets and shifting mix toward premium and value-added offerings. The total project cost is estimated at approximately Rs. 1,120 crores, funded through a mix of internal accruals and term debt; the Directors' Report locates the work at the Bhanwaria Kalan plant in Chittorgarh District, with debottlenecking equipment at the Hamirgarh plant in Bhilwara District, and states it is going on as per schedule. The project is expected to benefit from incentives under the Rajasthan Investment Promotion Scheme (RIPS) 2024, including interest subsidy, capital subsidy and electricity duty benefits. Alongside, the Company is implementing renewable captive power projects at a project cost of Rs. 230 crores, also progressing as scheduled: an additional 4.60 MW rooftop solar plant was installed at the Hamirgarh unit during the year taking total rooftop solar to 23.40 MW across both plants; a power purchase agreement for 28 MW of hybrid power under the group captive mechanism was signed, of which 18 MW began partial supply in FY 2025-26 with the remaining 10 MW to commence in FY 2026-27; a 33 MW solar power plant under open access is under installation at Chamu, district Jodhpur; and roof-top capacity of approximately 12 MW is under implementation at the Begun plant. After all these initiatives, renewable power consumption is expected to be more than 50% of the increased power consumption post completion of the expansion projects. Historically the Company added capacity in steps - the Begun Integrated Textile Complex with yarn manufacturing, processing, dyeing, printing and finishing was established in 2020, and a capex completed in 2024 installed 1,27,488 spindles, 264 airjet spinning positions, 3,312 rotors, 14 knitting machines, 54 weaving machines and 10 million metres per annum of finishing capacity.

Asset turn ~1:1 on new capex. **Watch H2 FY27 ramp timing.** RIPS incentives apply (capital subsidy 20-25/27% over 10 yrs; interest subsidy 5% term loan or 2.5% eligible FI for 5 yrs; electricity duty / mandi tax / land rebates).
capital allocation (debt): Net D/E down to 0.76x (from 0.89x). Balance financing via internal accruals + debt. Peak/normal total debt ~INR1,900-2,000 cr post-project (incl WC). Avg cost of borrowing ~5.6% (term), WC <7%, blended ~6.5%. Dividend INR3/share (30%).
risks:
- Cotton price: upward trend resuming; India-international parity dependence; lobbying for duty removal — outcome govt-dependent.
- China / export demand: West Asia/Iran-US conflict disrupting transit (esp. Europe) and freight; synthetic export logistics hit. US apparel inflation — a further 5-10% retail price rise could dent demand.
- Capex execution / ramp: H2 FY27 timing; ~INR1,900-2,000 cr peak debt.
- Knitted fabric: lost some US customers during tariff period; rebuild over 1-1.5 yrs.
- FTA timing slippage (EU another couple of quarters; duty removal uncertain).
mgmt tone: Confident and measured. "Highest ever quarterly revenue," constructive on demand recovery, FTAs and spread sustainability; firmly declined hard margin/segment-margin guidance (consistent 16-20% range repeated). Realistic on macro/tariff/inflation ("quite a macro question, very difficult to predict"). Declined inventory disclosure.
non-obvious:
- Spread INR90 floor should now be read as ~INR100 due to inflation in power/labor/component costs — re-rating of "normal" spread.
- China contribution to spread increase deliberately downplayed (10-11%→15-16% shipment share, not 30%+ of old) — mgmt won't attribute margin gain to China alone; restocking + transit-time fear + RM-cost floor are bigger drivers.
- Poly→cotton substitution thesis dismissed (cotton rose more than poly in INR/kg terms; poly still cheaper).
- Knit fabric weakness was tariff-driven (50% US tariff on low-value knits), now reversing.
- Renewable capex (INR230-240 cr) was unplanned add-on within the year.
challenges → beneficiaries:
- ✅ Beneficiary of US tariff normalization (10% vs feared 20-50%) and demand restocking.
- ⭐ Structural beneficiary of India-UK & India-EU FTAs (duty-disadvantage elimination, China+1 sourcing diversification to India) — finished-fabric and yarn demand uplift.
- ⭐ Beneficiary of domestic capacity rationalization (obsolete spinning capacity exited) supporting sustainable spreads.

themes.title: Textiles - apparel/home-textile exports + synthetics
themes.need: India textiles ride three tailwinds at once: China+1 sourcing shifts, the India-UK FTA (signed) + India-EU FTA (advancing), and US tariff normalization - favouring apparel exporters (GOKEX/PGIL/PDSL) and US-heavy home-textile names (WELSPUNLIV/HIMATSEIDE). A second leg = value-added synthetics/recycling (FILATEX, SANATHAN, CENTENKA, GANECOS) and cotton-yarn spread recovery (VTL/NITINSPIN/SPORTKING) plus branded apparel (PAGEIND, ARVIND, RAYMONDLSL).
themes.driver: FTA implementation + US-India trade-deal clarity; festive/wedding demand; cotton-yarn spread; anti-dumping rulings.

hero.oneLiner: Vertically-integrated cotton/blended yarn + fabric exporter delivering record quarterly revenue on demand recovery and yarn-spread expansion (~INR125/kg), with a large ~INR1,100 cr capex (spinning +22k t to ~130k t; fabric +35 mn m to ~75 mn m) commercializing H2 FY27 that should lift top line ~30-35% and shift mix toward higher-margin value-added/finished fabric.
